problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.prompt: Given an array of integers and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements.
problems.cue: 'Top k' plus 'you don't need them sorted among themselves' means a heap, not a sort. This is the single most likely pattern on a search team - every ranking stage is a top-k.
problems.approach: Count with a hash map, then take the k largest by count. A heap of size k keeps the work at n log k instead of n log n. If k is close to n, just sort. If you need it in O(n), quickselect on the counts.
problems.complexity: Time O(n log k), space O(n). Quickselect variant: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst.
edges: k equals the number of distinct elements
ties in frequency - ask whether the order among ties matters
problems.followup: Now the array is a stream you cannot hold in memory. (Count-Min Sketch plus a heap; discuss the approximation.)

problems.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
problems.prompt: Merge k sorted integer lists into one sorted list.
problems.cue: This is literally what an inverted index does when it merges postings lists. Say that out loud - it lands well on a search team.
problems.approach: Push the head of each list into a min-heap, pop the smallest, push that list's next element. The heap holds at most k items, so each of the n total elements costs one log k push and pop.
problems.complexity: Time O(n log k) for n total elements, space O(k).
problems.followup: The lists are on disk and do not fit in memory. (External merge; talk about buffer sizing and I/O.)

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
problems.prompt: Design a class that returns the kth largest element seen so far, supporting repeated add() calls.
problems.cue: 'Stream' plus 'kth largest' means a bounded min-heap. The counter-intuitive part - min-heap for largest - is the whole trick.
problems.approach: Keep a min-heap of exactly k elements. Its root is the kth largest. On add, push and pop if the size exceeds k. Trim in the constructor too, which is the step people forget.
problems.complexity: Time O(log k) per add, O(n log k) to construct. Space O(k).
edges: fewer than k elements at construction
problems.followup: Now support removal of an arbitrary element. (Heap plus lazy deletion, or a balanced BST / SortedList.)

problems.title: Implement Trie
problems.prompt: Implement a trie with insert, search, and startsWith.
problems.cue: Any prefix question. On a search team the trie is the autocomplete data structure, so expect this as a warm-up before the real question.
problems.approach: A dict of dicts, with a sentinel key marking the end of a word. Factor the shared walk into one helper so search and startsWith differ by one line - interviewers notice that.
problems.complexity: Time O(L) per operation for a word of length L. Space O(total characters inserted).
edges: search a prefix that is not itself a word
problems.followup: Add delete. (Reference-count the nodes, or prune upward while the node has no children and no sentinel.)

problems.title: Search Suggestions System
problems.prompt: Given a list of products and a search word, return the three lexicographically smallest products with each prefix of the search word, as the user types.
problems.cue: This is typeahead. Coupang's job posting names 'query recommendation' explicitly, so this exact problem is fair game.
problems.approach: Two clean options. Sort the products and binary search the prefix each keystroke, scanning at most three past the insertion point. Or build a trie and store the three smallest completions at each node. The sorted-array version is shorter and usually what you want under time pressure; the trie version is what you say scales to a real system.
problems.complexity: Sorted: O(n log n) to sort, then O(log n + 3) per keystroke. Trie: O(total chars) to build, O(L) to query.
edges: no matches for a prefix - and every later prefix also has none
problems.followup: Rank by popularity rather than lexicographically. (Store a top-3 heap per trie node; discuss how updates propagate.)

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.prompt: Given two strings, return the minimum number of insertions, deletions, or substitutions to turn one into the other.
problems.cue: The classic DP, and the algorithm behind spell correction - which is a query-understanding component you should be able to connect it to.
problems.approach: dp[i][j] is the distance between the first i characters of a and the first j of b. Either the last characters match and you inherit dp[i-1][j-1], or you pay one for the best of insert, delete, substitute. Roll the table to one row to get linear space.
problems.complexity: Time O(mn), space O(min(m,n)) with the rolling row.
problems.followup: Only report whether the distance is at most 2. (Band the DP to a diagonal of width 2k+1 - O(kn) instead of O(mn). This is the optimisation real spell correctors use.)

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.prompt: Group a list of words so that anagrams of one another are in the same group.
problems.cue: 'Group by some canonical form' - the whole problem is choosing the key. Warm-up difficulty; do not overthink it.
problems.approach: Canonicalise each word by sorting its characters and bucket by that key. A 26-length count tuple is the O(L) alternative to the O(L log L) sort, and worth mentioning even if you write the sort.
problems.complexity: Time O(n L log L), or O(n L) with count keys. Space O(n L).
edges: unicode - the count-vector trick assumes a fixed small alphabet
problems.followup: Now the alphabet is unicode and words are long. (Count keys stop being cheap; hash a frozen Counter, and discuss collisions.)

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.prompt: Return the length of the longest substring with no repeated characters.
problems.cue: Sliding window with a hash map. The bug everyone writes is moving the left pointer backwards.
problems.approach: Track the last index of each character. When you see a repeat whose last index is at or after the window start, jump the start to one past it. Never move the start backwards - that guard is the correctness condition.
problems.complexity: Time O(n), space O(alphabet).
edges: the repeat lies before the current window start - the case the guard exists for
problems.followup: Allow at most k distinct characters. (Same window, but shrink on distinct count rather than on repeats.)

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.prompt: Given strings s and t, return the shortest substring of s containing every character of t including duplicates.
problems.cue: Variable-size sliding window with a need-counter. One of the highest-value hard problems to have rehearsed, because the pattern generalises.
problems.approach: Counter of what you still need. Expand the right edge, decrementing; a character was needed if its count was positive before the decrement. When nothing is missing, contract the left edge while recording the best window. The sign convention on the counter is what makes this short.
problems.complexity: Time O(|s| + |t|), space O(|t|).
edges: t has duplicate characters - the reason it is a counter and not a set
problems.followup: Return all minimum windows, not one. (Keep a list at the current best length, reset it when you find shorter.)

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.prompt: Find a target in a sorted array that has been rotated at an unknown pivot. O(log n).
problems.cue: Binary search where the invariant is broken. At every midpoint, one of the two halves is still sorted - find which, and decide from there.
problems.approach: Compare nums[lo] with nums[mid]. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid] the left half is sorted, so check whether the target lies inside that sorted range; otherwise the right half is sorted and you check that range. Getting the <= right at the boundary is the whole problem.
problems.complexity: Time O(log n), space O(1).
edges: duplicates - which break O(log n) and need a separate discussion
problems.followup: Now there are duplicates. (Worst case degrades to O(n); explain why you cannot tell which half is sorted when nums[lo] == nums[mid].)

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
problems.prompt: Given an n x n matrix where each row and column is sorted ascending, return the kth smallest element.
problems.cue: When a heap solution is obvious but the constraints are large, look for binary search on the answer value rather than on an index. That reframing is the thing being tested.
problems.approach: Binary search over the value range. For a candidate value, count how many entries are at most it by walking from the bottom-left corner - move right when the entry fits, up when it does not, O(n) per probe. Then narrow. The answer is always an actual matrix entry because the search converges to the smallest value with count at least k.
problems.complexity: Time O(n log(max - min)), space O(1). The heap alternative is O(k log n).
problems.followup: Why is the converged value guaranteed to be in the matrix? (Because the predicate count(x) >= k first becomes true exactly at a matrix value.)

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.prompt: Given a list of intervals, merge all overlapping ones.
problems.cue: Almost every interval problem starts with 'sort by start'. Say that first and the rest follows.
problems.approach: Sort by start. Walk through, and either the current interval starts within the last merged one - extend its end to the max - or it does not, and you append. Copy the intervals before mutating, or you will corrupt the caller's input.
problems.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).
edges: touching but not overlapping - ask whether [1,4] and [4,5] merge
problems.followup: Insert a new interval into an already-merged list in O(n). (Three phases: before, overlapping, after.)
problems.code:
def min_meeting_rooms(intervals):
    if not intervals:
        return 0
    starts = sorted(i[0] for i in intervals)
    ends = sorted(i[1] for i in intervals)
    rooms = best = 0
    j = 0
    for s in starts:
        while j < len(ends) and ends[j] <= s:
            rooms -= 1
            j += 1
        rooms += 1
        best = max(best, rooms)
    return best

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
problems.prompt: Given meeting intervals, return the minimum number of rooms required.
problems.cue: 'Maximum concurrent' means either a sweep line or a min-heap of end times. The sweep is shorter to write.
problems.approach: Sort starts and ends into two separate arrays. Sweep the starts; before each, release every room whose end time is at or before it. Track the running count and its maximum. Equivalently, a min-heap of end times - same complexity, more code.
problems.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).
edges: a meeting ending exactly when another starts - ask if that shares a room
problems.followup: Return which meeting goes in which room. (Heap of (end_time, room_id) - the sweep loses that information.)

problems.title: Course Schedule
problems.prompt: Given a number of courses and prerequisite pairs, determine whether all courses can be finished.
problems.cue: 'Can this be ordered' means cycle detection in a directed graph - Kahn's algorithm. The dependency-resolution problem in disguise.
problems.approach: Build the adjacency list and in-degree array. Queue every zero in-degree node, pop, decrement its neighbours, enqueue any that hit zero. If you processed every node there is no cycle. Get the edge direction right - prerequisite points to course.
problems.complexity: Time O(V + E), space O(V + E).
problems.followup: Return a valid order, not just whether one exists. (Same algorithm; collect the pop order.)

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.prompt: Count connected components of '1' cells in a 2D grid.
problems.cue: Grid plus connectivity means flood fill. The only real decision is recursive or iterative.
problems.approach: Scan every cell; on an unvisited '1', flood fill and increment the count. Write it iteratively with an explicit stack - a 1000x1000 grid of all ones will blow the Python recursion limit, and saying so unprompted is worth a point.
problems.complexity: Time O(rows * cols), space O(rows * cols) worst case for the stack.
problems.followup: The grid does not fit in memory. (Union-find over row stripes; or discuss a streaming two-pass connected-component labelling.)

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.prompt: Given a start word, an end word, and a dictionary, return the length of the shortest transformation sequence changing one letter at a time.
problems.cue: 'Shortest' on an unweighted graph is BFS, always. The graph is implicit - you generate neighbours rather than store edges.
problems.approach: BFS from the start. Neighbours are every word one substitution away that is in the dictionary. Mark visited when you enqueue, not when you dequeue, or the queue fills with duplicates. Generating 26L candidates per word beats comparing against every dictionary word when the dictionary is large.
problems.complexity: Time O(N * L * 26) where N is dictionary size and L word length. Space O(N * L).
edges: end word not in the dictionary - return 0 immediately
problems.followup: Make it bidirectional BFS. (Search from both ends, expand the smaller frontier; roughly squares down the branching.)

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.prompt: Given coin denominations and an amount, return the fewest coins that make that amount, or -1.
problems.cue: The canonical unbounded knapsack. Coupang's own interview guidance names dynamic programming explicitly, so have one of these fluent.
problems.approach: dp[a] is the fewest coins for amount a. dp[0] is zero; for each amount try each coin and take one plus dp[a - coin]. Use amount+1 as the infinity sentinel so you never overflow and the final check is clean. Greedy is wrong here and you should say why - denominations like 1, 3, 4 making 6.
problems.complexity: Time O(amount * coins), space O(amount).
edges: amount zero - answer is zero, not -1
a coin larger than the amount
problems.followup: Count the number of ways instead of the minimum. (Same table, but the loop order flips - coins outside, amounts inside - or you count permutations instead of combinations.)

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.prompt: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
problems.cue: The O(n^2) DP is the obvious answer; the O(n log n) patience-sorting version is the one that separates candidates.
problems.approach: Maintain a 'tails' array where tails[i] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length i+1. For each number, binary search its position and either extend or overwrite. The array is not itself a valid subsequence - say that before they ask, because it shows you understand rather than memorised.
problems.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).
edges: all equal - bisect_left gives strictly increasing, bisect_right gives non-decreasing
problems.followup: Reconstruct the actual subsequence. (Store predecessor indices alongside; the tails array alone cannot reconstruct it.)

problems.title: LRU Cache
problems.prompt: Design a cache with O(1) get and put that evicts the least recently used entry at capacity.
problems.cue: The most-asked design-flavoured coding question there is. On a search team it is also real - your query-rewrite cache is exactly this.
problems.approach: Hash map plus doubly linked list: the map gives O(1) lookup, the list gives O(1) reordering. In Python, OrderedDict with move_to_end and popitem(last=False) is that structure - use it, but be ready to write the linked list by hand, because some interviewers require it.
problems.complexity: Time O(1) for both operations, space O(capacity).
edges: updating an existing key - it counts as a use
get on a missing key must not insert
problems.followup: Make it thread-safe, or make it LFU instead. (LFU needs frequency buckets with a min-frequency pointer.)

problems.title: Rank products by a composite key
problems.prompt: Sort products by relevance score descending, then rating descending, then price ascending, then id ascending as a deterministic tie-break.
problems.cue: Not a hard problem - a correctness-and-care problem, which is exactly what Coupang says it grades. Expect it as a warm-up or embedded in a larger question.
problems.approach: One sort with a tuple key, negating the descending numeric fields. Do not chain multiple sorts unless you are deliberately relying on stability, and if you do, say so. The final id tie-break matters in production: without it, equal-scoring products shuffle between requests and your A/B test picks up noise.
problems.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).
edges: ties across every field - the id makes the order total
floating-point score equality, which is why you want an explicit final key
problems.followup: The scores come from a model and are float32. How do you make ranking stable across replicas? (Round to a fixed precision before sorting, or rank by a deterministic key; discuss why float non-determinism across hardware is real.)
